mcqs.q: Enamel is best described as the:
opts: Hardest calcified tissue in the body, covering the anatomic crown
mcqs.explain: Enamel is the hardest calcified tissue in the human body and forms the protective covering of the anatomical crown.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE of enamel structure?
opts: It contains no cells, blood vessels, nerves or collagen
mcqs.explain: Enamel is a unique calcified epithelial tissue with no cells, blood vessels, nerves or collagen; mature enamel is acellular, avascular and non-vital.

mcqs.q: Enamel is formed by which cells?
mcqs.explain: Enamel is derived from ectoderm and made by ameloblasts (the inner enamel epithelium of the enamel organ).

mcqs.q: A key clinical point about enamel is that it:
opts: Cannot regenerate (the forming cells are lost)
mcqs.explain: Because the ameloblasts are lost after enamel formation, enamel cannot regenerate and must be preserved.

mcqs.q: Enamel is thickest at the:
opts: Incisal edge and cusp tips (2–2.5 mm), thinning to a knife-edge cervically
mcqs.explain: Enamel is 2–2.5 mm thick at the incisal edge/cusp tips and ends cervically as a knife-edge.

mcqs.q: The yellowish appearance of thinner enamel is because it:
opts: Becomes translucent and reflects the yellow dentin beneath
mcqs.explain: Thick enamel is opaque greyish-white; as it thins it becomes translucent and reflects the colour of the underlying yellow dentin.

mcqs.q: Enamel hardness INCREASES with:
mcqs.explain: Enamel is hard due to its high inorganic content and crystalline arrangement; hardness increases with fluoride application.

mcqs.q: Regarding tensile strength, enamel is:
opts: Low in tensile strength and brittle, depending on the underlying dentin
High in tensile strength and flexible
mcqs.explain: Enamel has low tensile strength (less than dentin) and is brittle; its integrity depends on the support of the underlying dentin.

mcqs.q: By WEIGHT, the inorganic content of enamel is about:
mcqs.explain: Enamel is ~96% inorganic (hydroxyapatite) by weight and ~4% water and organic material.

mcqs.q: The main inorganic component of enamel is:
mcqs.explain: Enamel is composed almost entirely of hydroxyapatite crystals (calcium + phosphate) — the largest crystals of any calcified tissue.

mcqs.q: The MAIN organic protein of enamel (about 90%) is:
mcqs.explain: Amelogenins make up ~90% of the enamel proteins (low molecular weight); non-amelogenins (~10%) include enamelin, ameloblastin and tuftelin. There is NO collagen.

mcqs.q: Enamel must be studied under the microscope as a:
opts: Ground section (decalcified sections would dissolve it)
mcqs.explain: Because enamel is highly mineralized, it is studied as a ground section; a decalcified section would dissolve the enamel away.

mcqs.q: The basic structural unit of enamel is the:
mcqs.explain: The enamel rod (prism) is the basic fundamental unit — a cylinder packed with hydroxyapatite crystals.

mcqs.q: The number of enamel rods in a tooth ranges from about:
mcqs.explain: Enamel rods number from ~5 million (lower lateral incisor) to ~12 million (upper first permanent molar).

mcqs.q: On cross-section/EM, enamel rods show a characteristic:
opts: 'Keyhole' (fish-scale) shape with a head/body and tail
mcqs.explain: Enamel rods have a keyhole/fish-scale appearance — a head/body (nearer the occlusal surface) and a tail pointing cervically.

mcqs.q: The region between enamel rods, with crystals of a DIFFERENT orientation, is the:
mcqs.explain: Between rods is the inter-rod (interprismatic) region, whose crystals have a different orientation; the rod sheath surrounds each rod.

mcqs.q: The rod (prism) sheath is characterised by:
opts: Less densely packed crystals and more enamel protein
mcqs.explain: The rod sheath surrounds each rod and contains less densely packed crystals (and more enamel proteins).

mcqs.q: Cross striations of enamel rods represent:
mcqs.explain: Each rod is built of uniform ~4 µm segments separated by dark lines (cross striations), representing about a day's growth.

mcqs.q: Gnarled enamel is found where the rods:
opts: Twist and swirl around each other at cusp tips and incisal edges
mcqs.explain: At cusp tips and incisal edges the rods twist/swirl around each other — gnarled enamel — giving extra resistance to fracture under heavy chewing.

mcqs.q: Why is gnarled enamel important?
opts: It makes enamel more resistant to fracture in areas of heavy force
mcqs.explain: The interwoven (twisted) arrangement of gnarled enamel increases fracture resistance, especially at cusps and incisal edges.

mcqs.q: The enamel hydroxyapatite crystals are notable for being:
opts: The largest of all calcified tissues, hexagonal in cross-section
The smallest crystals in the body
mcqs.explain: Enamel hydroxyapatite crystals are the largest of any calcified tissue and are hexagonal in cross-section.

mcqs.q: The permeability of enamel changes with age by:
mcqs.explain: Enamel is selectively permeable through microscopic pores/cracks; permeability decreases and hardness increases with age.

saqs.q: Define enamel and give its unique features.
saqs.a: The hardest calcified tissue, covering the anatomic crown. Unique: a calcified epithelial tissue with no cells, vessels, nerves or collagen; made by ameloblasts; cannot regenerate.

saqs.q: Describe the physical properties of enamel.
saqs.a: Thickness 2–2.5 mm at cusps/incisal, knife-edge cervically. Colour greyish-white (thick) → yellowish (thin, reflects dentin). Hardest (↑ with fluoride) but low tensile strength/brittle; selectively permeable.

saqs.q: Give the chemical composition of enamel.
saqs.a: 96% inorganic (hydroxyapatite — Ca/phosphate + ions). 4% water & organic: proteins (no collagen) — amelogenins (90%) + non-amelogenins (enamelin, ameloblastin, tuftelin).

saqs.q: Why and how is enamel studied as a ground section?
saqs.a: Enamel is too hard/mineralized for routine decalcified sections (which dissolve it), so it is studied as a ground section.

saqs.q: Describe the enamel rod and its components.
saqs.a: The basic unit — a cylinder of hydroxyapatite crystals running a wavy course DEJ→surface, with a keyhole shape (head/body + tail). Between rods is the inter-rod region; each rod has a rod sheath (less-packed crystals).

saqs.q: What are cross striations of enamel rods?
saqs.a: Dark lines dividing each rod into uniform ~4 µm segments, representing about one day's growth (4 µm/day).

saqs.q: What is gnarled enamel and why is it important?
saqs.a: At cusp tips and incisal edges, enamel rods twist and swirl around each other; this interwoven arrangement increases resistance to fracture under heavy chewing forces.
